intro: Chiang Rai is a city that packs contemporary art, extraordinary temples, vast tea fields, and an evening market all into one province. Drive just a few minutes from town and you hit landmarks that have defined northern Thailand on the map. We've picked 10 places people rarely skip when they visit — from the gleaming white Wat Rong Khun to the Saturday Walking Street — so anyone planning a trip has a clear starting point.
chips: 🚗 Full city loop in a single day

blocks.html:
If you haven't been to Chiang Rai before, this city is more easygoing than you might expect. The main attractions cluster in a manageable radius around the town center. Start your morning at Wat Rong Khun in the Pa O Don Chai area, loop over to the blue-hued Wat Rong Suea Ten by the Kok River, swing through Singha Park's wide tea fields in Mae Kan during midday, then ease back into the old town along Thanalai Road for the Walking Street. The air here is cooler than central Thailand year-round — you can walk and shoot photos all day without feeling rushed.

Chiang Rai's real charm is art you can actually touch. Wat Rong Khun is the decades-long project of artist Chalermchai Kositpipat — still under construction, still jaw-dropping, now the province's defining image. Baan Dam Museum is the life's work of National Artist Thawan Duchanee: over 40 Lanna-style blackwood buildings crammed with carved wooden sculptures and rare objects. Wat Huay Pla Kang has a massive Guan Yin statue on a hill with a lift to the top and panoramic city views. And the Chalermchai-designed Clock Tower in the city center puts on a free light show after dark. Come for the temples, stay for the tea and the night markets — you won't leave disappointed.

blocks.name: Wat Rong Khun (White Temple)
blocks.area: Pa O Don Chai, Mueang Chiang Rai District
blocks.signature: All-white temple encrusted with mirror glass, a bridge over sculpted hands rising from below, and intricately carved plasterwork on every surface
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Rong Khun — known internationally as the White Temple — is a fully white structure studded with tiny mirror fragments that catch the sunlight like a building made of glass. Artist Chalermchai Kositpipat began designing and building it in 1997 and the work continues to this day, never declared finished. The symbolism is Buddhist purity. For anyone who loves art, photography, or is visiting Chiang Rai for the first time, this is virtually a mandatory stop — and one of the most talked-about attractions in the entire North.

The highlight you can't miss is the bridge to the ubosot. In front of the bridge, hundreds of sculpted hands reach upward from below, representing desire and hell. Walking across it feels like crossing out of suffering into a purer realm. The ubosot itself is plastered in elaborate detail — nagas, contemporary Thai motifs, mirror glass winking in every direction. The murals inside are contemporary Buddhist art unlike anything you'd find elsewhere. For the best photos with fewer crowds, most visitors recommend arriving right when it opens in the morning or in the late afternoon around 16:30 when the light turns soft and the mirror panels glow.

Entry is free for Thais; foreigners pay admission (100 THB previously, subject to adjustment in 2026). Open daily 08:00–17:00. Located in Pa O Don Chai along Phahonyothin Road toward Mae Lao, about 13 km from central Chiang Rai — less than 20 minutes by car. There's a large car park, restaurants, souvenir stalls, and local fabric shops surrounding the site. Budget roughly 1–2 hours to walk the grounds comfortably.

The temple stays popular because there is simply nothing else like it in Thai Buddhist art. Reviews consistently praise how striking it is, how well-organized, how clean. The heat and the crowds peak during high season — bring a hat or umbrella, dress respectfully since it is an active temple, and don't touch the plasterwork. Follow the signage about where photography is and isn't permitted, and don't block the bridge for other visitors.
mustOrder: Bridge to the ubosot + sculpted hands rising from hell
All-white temple encrusted with mirror glass
Contemporary plasterwork and murals inside
Late-afternoon light for photography
blocks.bestFor: First-time visitors, photography and art lovers

blocks.name: Wat Rong Suea Ten (Blue Temple)
blocks.area: Rim Kok, Mueang Chiang Rai District, Chiang Rai
blocks.signature: Cobalt-blue-and-gold ubosot, a pair of naga serpents flanking the entrance, and a luminous white Buddha glowing against the deep blue interior
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Rong Suea Ten — known as the Blue Temple — has firmly established itself as a Chiang Rai landmark alongside the White Temple. It sits on the east side of the city by the Kok River, about 10 minutes from the center. Anyone who loves photographing beautiful temples or wants to pay respects in an atmosphere unlike any other will want to make this a definite stop. The ubosot was designed by local artist "Sla Nak" Phuttha Kabkaew, who previously collaborated with Chalermchai Kositpipat at Wat Rong Khun — so you feel that same contemporary-Thai-art intensity.

The highlight you can't miss is the cobalt-blue ubosot trimmed with gold. The entire building is coated in deep, vivid blue with golden detailing tracing the patterns. Step inside and a white-pearl main Buddha image stands brilliantly lit against the dark blue surround — the contrast is what makes photos from this temple come out so well from almost any angle. The ceiling carries detailed Buddhist murals. Out front, a pair of blue naga serpents flank the entrance in the most-photographed spot, and a large white Buddha sits at the rear.

Free entry. Open daily approximately 07:00–20:00. The temple opens its lights in the evening, giving the blue a deeper, more solemn quality. TripAdvisor consistently ranks it among the top attractions in Chiang Rai, with around 4.5 stars. The main feedback: come early in the morning when it opens, or in the late afternoon, to get clean photos without tour groups. The whole visit takes 20–30 minutes, making it easy to combine with Wat Rong Khun or Singha Park in a single trip. Dress modestly. There's lift access for visitors with limited mobility.

Key tip: midday sees the most tour buses. Photos and a contemplative visit both work best in the morning or the cooler evening hours.
mustOrder: Cobalt-blue-and-gold ubosot
White-pearl main Buddha inside the ubosot
Naga-serpent pair flanking the entrance
Large white Buddha at the rear
blocks.bestFor: Photography lovers visiting temples in the morning or evening
blocks.zone: Rim Kok (east side of the city)

blocks.name: Singha Park Chiang Rai (Singha Park)
blocks.area: Mae Kan, Mueang Chiang Rai District
blocks.signature: Expansive grounds, rows of Oolong tea fields, seasonal flower gardens, farm tour tram, cycling, and a hot-air balloon photo spot
blocks.priceRange: Free entry; activities priced separately — tram ~50–150 THB
blocks.descHtml:
Singha Park Chiang Rai — formerly known as Boon Rawd Farm — is a vast agritourism estate of several thousand rai to the southwest of the city, about 9 km from the center. The draw is the sheer openness: rolling rows of Oolong tea stretching as far as you can see, seasonal flower gardens that rotate throughout the year, and the giant hot-air balloon that has become the park's signature photo landmark. Ideal for families with mixed ages, groups of friends who love photography, and anyone wanting wide-open green space without elbow-to-elbow crowds.

The highlight most visitors talk about is the farm tour tram that circles the property, stopping at the lake, a tea-tasting station, the flower garden zones, and the mini zoo where you can get close to giraffes and zebras for hand feeding. For more active visitors there's cycling, a zip line, and golf carts to rent. International reviewers give it around 4.1 stars from thousands of reviews, praising the natural setting, the organization, and the tram that runs every 15 minutes with tea samples thrown in.

Budget-friendly: entry is free, but activities are priced separately. The tram starts at a few dozen to a few hundred baht per person. Golf carts run around 500–600 THB to rent, bicycles are priced by the hour in the hundreds, and the zip line is around 300 THB. Open daily approximately 09:00–17:00; the tram runs 09:30–17:00. One note: if you visit outside flower season, some zones may be emptier than the photos suggest.

The park works well as a half-day or full-day outing — you get tea fields, the balloon photo spot, animal feeding, and a cool cup of tea all in one place. Come in the morning or late afternoon when the sun is gentler and the light is better for photos. Bring a hat and water — it's wide open and shade is limited.
mustOrder: Farm tour tram through the tea fields
Hot-air balloon photo spot
Giraffe and zebra feeding at the mini zoo
Jinxuan Oolong tea tasting
blocks.bestFor: Families and groups, tea field photography, morning or late afternoon

blocks.name: Wat Huay Pla Kang
blocks.area: Rim Kok, Mueang District, Chiang Rai
blocks.signature: Towering white Guan Yin statue on a hilltop, a 9-storey pagoda with a lift to the top, and a white dragon staircase
blocks.priceRange: Free (lift to the Guan Yin statue — 40 THB)
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Huay Pla Kang sits on a small hill to the northwest of Chiang Rai city, about 6 km from the center, and has become an essential stop for visitors. The landmark you can see from afar is a towering white Guan Yin statue (around 69 meters tall) designed so that visitors can ride a lift up through the interior and gaze out from the statue's eyes at floor 25–26, taking in a panoramic view of the city. Ideal for people who want both merit-making and sweeping views in one stop — whether you're drawn to spiritual sites, photography, or bringing older family members to pay respects.

Three highlights stand out clearly. First is the 9-storey Great Pagoda (Phop Chok Tham Chedi), Chinese-Lanna hybrid architecture with Buddha images and Guan Yin across each floor — walk up level by level to reach extraordinary views at the top. Second is the Guan Yin statue itself: take the lift up to look out through the statue's eyes. Third is the white naga-dragon staircase leading up to the Guan Yin plaza — photogenic from every angle. Multiple reviews agree that the temple is clean, the staff are friendly, and the grounds are more spacious than expected.

Entry is free; offerings are voluntary. The lift to the Guan Yin statue costs 40 THB per person — almost every visitor says it's worth it for the view. Inside the grounds there's a food and drinks stall with very affordable prices (reviews mention pad thai at 20 THB per plate) plus a shuttle and lift service, making the grounds easy to navigate even in strong sun. Plan for 1–2 hours.

Open daily approximately 07:00–21:30. Address: 553 Moo 3, Rim Kok, Mueang, Chiang Rai. The temple is popular because it packs a large statue, a tall pagoda, city views, and photo opportunities all into one visit. Google rating reaches 4.7 from over 16,000 reviews. The midmorning-to-afternoon window gets busy and hot — mornings and late afternoons near sunset are quieter and more photogenic. Dress modestly.
mustOrder: 9-storey Great Pagoda (Phop Chok Tham Chedi)
Lift to the top of the Guan Yin statue — 40 THB
White naga-dragon staircase
Panoramic view of Chiang Rai from the top floor
blocks.bestFor: Morning or evening temple visit, photography, and city views

blocks.name: Baan Dam Museum (Black House)
blocks.area: Nang Lae, Mueang Chiang Rai District
blocks.signature: Over 40 black Lanna-style wooden buildings housing animal horns, hides, and carved wood sculptures — the life's work of National Artist Thawan Duchanee
blocks.descHtml:
Baan Dam Museum — known internationally as the Black House — is the life's work of Thawan Duchanee, National Artist in Visual Arts. It sits on over 100 rai in Nang Lae subdistrict along Phahonyothin Road toward Mae Chan. Inside are more than 40 Lanna-style dark-wood buildings of completely different shapes — some tall wooden chapel forms, some small standalone houses in open fields. The place is made for people who love art and architecture, and for anyone who wants to see the polar opposite of the gleaming White Temple. Chiang Rai locals like to say: the White Temple is heaven, and Baan Dam is the dark and solemn counterpoint.

The must-see is the collection inside each building: animal horns and hides, bones, silverwork, and large carved wooden sculptures that Thawan used as artistic elements. The largest building — a cathedral-like structure — took years to build. Inside, a long table draped with animal hide and framed by skeletal forms is the shot that most visitors take first. Reviews consistently describe the atmosphere as lush and leafy, easy to walk through and rest in, with the art being raw and intense. Some visitors love it immediately; others find the animal elements unsettling. That discomfort is part of what makes this place irreplaceable.

Entry is 80 THB per person. Open daily 09:00–17:00. Plan 1–2 hours. Located about 12 km north of the city center — easy by car or chartered songthaew. Many visitors combine it with Wat Rong Khun and Wat Rong Suea Ten in a single day's circuit. Google reviews hold it at around 4.5 stars. The grounds are open-air between buildings, so midday sun can be strong — bring a hat and wear comfortable shoes. Some buildings can only be viewed from outside. The themes center on death and truth, so if you're bringing young children, prepare them gently for the animal elements.
mustOrder: Black wooden cathedral — the largest building
Long table with animal hide and skeletal display
40+ black Lanna wooden buildings
Thawan Duchanee's carved wood sculptures
blocks.bestFor: Art and architecture lovers, pairing with Wat Rong Khun on the same day

blocks.title: 🛏️ Where to Stay in Chiang Rai — Easy Booking, Easy Exploring
blocks.text: Staying in central Chiang Rai means you can get to Wat Rong Khun before the crowds and walk to the Saturday Walking Street and Night Bazaar without a long drive. The Clock Tower area and the Kok River bank have hotels and guesthouses across a range of budgets. Book ahead for the cool-season end-of-year period when rooms go fast.

blocks.name: Central Chiangrai
blocks.area: Rob Wiang, Mueang Chiang Rai District
blocks.signature: The province's largest mall — shops, a cinema, food court, and a Lanna-themed zone inside
blocks.descHtml:
If you want one place in Chiang Rai to shop, eat, catch a film, escape the heat, and escape the rain, Central Chiangrai is what locals reach for first. It's the province's largest mall, sitting on Phahonyothin Road near the town center — a multi-storey building with major brands throughout: Tops supermarket, Robinson, Starbucks, Boots, clothing stores, mobile phone shops, banks, all under one roof. Great for families, travelers who need a break from temple-hopping, or anyone who wants to pick up gifts and supplies in air-conditioned comfort.

The highlight many visitors mention is the cinema, which screens both Thai films and foreign films with Thai subtitles — and international visitors appreciate the English-dubbed screenings. The food court is a real draw too: foreign reviewers consistently praise the food here as tasty and fairly priced, especially the khao soi and northern Thai dishes. The mall has also leaned into its Lanna identity, with Lanna-styled decorative zones and a events space that hosts rotating food festivals throughout the year, giving it a flavor beyond a standard shopping center.

No entry fee — browse freely, spend as little or as much as you like. The food court dishes start at a few tens of baht; sit-down restaurants inside run higher. Location on Phahonyothin Road makes it easy to reach by taxi or motorbike taxi. Open daily approximately 10:30–21:00 (Sat–Sun from 10:00). One practical note: the car park fills up fast on public holidays and long weekends — if you're coming then, factor in extra time to park.

Google rating holds at 4.5 from several thousand reviews — a genuine community hub, not just a tourist convenience. Most reviewers praise how clean, spacious, and well-organized it is, with good air conditioning. Works equally well as a quick rest stop mid-trip or a comfortable half-day. Families will find a kids' play zone and game machines, too.
mustOrder: Cinema showing English-dubbed and Thai-subtitled films
Food court — khao soi and northern Thai dishes
Lanna-themed decor zone
Tops supermarket for souvenirs and local products
blocks.bestFor: Families, shopping and a film, escaping the heat

blocks.name: Chiang Rai Walking Street (Kad Jia Hay Ramluk)
blocks.area: Thanalai Road, Wiang, Mueang Chiang Rai District
blocks.signature: Saturday evening market with northern Thai street food, handmade crafts, traditional clothing, and a folk-dance performance stage
blocks.descHtml:
If your Chiang Rai visit happens to fall on a Saturday evening, this is not something to skip. Chiang Rai Walking Street — officially Kad Jia Hay Ramluk — runs along Thanalai Road in the old city center, close to the Clock Tower. It sets up from early evening and stretches for a full kilometer with over 200 stalls on both sides. Ideal for anyone who wants to eat their way through northern Thai food, browse handmade goods, and absorb the Lanna way of life in one place. International visitors appreciate that most of the crowd is actually local Chiang Rai residents, making the whole thing feel like a real community market rather than a performance for outsiders.

The highlights most people mention are the vintage folk-dance stage, where elderly residents and young people alike join traditional ram wong circle dances, with live folk music playing throughout. The food is the real draw — northern Thai originals lined up everywhere: grilled skewers and smoky barbecue, traditional snacks, fruit, unusual sweets. Multiple foreign reviewers agree: the food is cheap, fresh, and you could eat your way through the whole evening, dish by dish. A second zone runs handmade crafts, tribal textiles, traditional clothing, home décor, and souvenirs, with clear price tags on everything — no exhausting bargaining needed.

Free entry, no admission. Bring small Thai baht cash — mostly cash-only stalls. The ATMs nearby sometimes run dry; carry enough before you arrive. Within easy walking distance of most hotels in the old town. Open Saturday evenings only, approximately 16:00–22:00. Peak crowd time is around 19:00–20:00; if you want to browse comfortably and not miss anything, arriving around 17:00 is ideal.

Google rating at 4.5 from several thousand reviews. Key tip: Sunday also has a separate Walking Street on a different road if you want a second outing, but Kad Jia Hay Ramluk on Saturday is the definitive northern food and folk-dance experience.
mustOrder: Grilled skewers and northern Thai street food
Vintage folk-dance stage and live folk music
Handmade crafts, tribal textiles, and traditional clothing
Traditional local snacks and sweets
blocks.bestFor: Saturday evening dinner, eating northern Thai food and watching folk performances
blocks.zone: Old city (Thanalai Road, near the Clock Tower)

blocks.name: Chiang Rai Night Bazaar
blocks.signature: Open-every-night market with a central food court and live performance stage, plus a handcraft and local product shopping zone
blocks.descHtml:
Chiang Rai Night Bazaar is the city-center night market that opens every single evening, right next to the old bus terminal, within easy walking distance of most downtown hotels. It's often the first stop people make on arrival in Chiang Rai — there's food, souvenirs, and live performances all in one compact place. Works well for travelers who've just checked in and want a simple, no-fuss dinner spot, as well as for anyone who wants to pick up local handicrafts and textiles. It's not as large as the Chiang Mai Night Bazaar, but many visitors say that's actually the appeal — it's easy to navigate, not crushingly crowded, and the pace is relaxed.

The highlight you can't miss is the central food court with a live performance stage: bands, singers, and traditional local dancing in regional costumes. You pick food from whichever stall you like and sit at shared tables in front of the stage. Quite a few real reviews single out the food zone as the best part, praising the variety, freshness, and low prices — with at least one reviewer calling it the best food court they'd encountered anywhere in Thailand. The second zone is handcrafted goods, handmade T-shirts, artwork, and local products made by villagers and ethnic-minority communities, typically at lower prices than other tourist markets.

Free entry; you pay only for what you eat or buy. Dinner for two runs around 100 THB. The atmosphere is warm, the lighting is inviting, and music from the stage runs all evening. Open daily approximately 18:00 through around 23:00; weekends are livelier than weekdays.

Google score sits at 4.2 from over 14,000 reviews — a reliable indicator that most visitors leave satisfied. Practical note: if you want a seat right in front of the stage, arrive early evening before the peak hour. If you want a bigger market experience, the Saturday Walking Street is nearby on weekends — but for an every-night dinner option and live performance, the Night Bazaar is the go-to.
mustOrder: Central food court in front of the live performance stage
Traditional local dance and live music
Handcrafts and local products
blocks.bestFor: First night in the city + live performances

blocks.name: Chiang Rai Royal Jubilee Clock Tower
blocks.area: Wiang, Mueang Chiang Rai District, Chiang Rai
blocks.signature: Gold-toned clock tower designed by Chalermchai Kositpipat, with a light and color show set to music on three fixed nightly schedules
blocks.descHtml:
The Chiang Rai Royal Jubilee Clock Tower — known locally as the Chiang Rai Clock Tower — is the central landmark that almost every visitor photographs at least once. It stands in the middle of the Ban Prapakarn intersection roundabout, designed by Chalermchai Kositpipat, the same artist behind Wat Rong Khun. The same gold-tinged Buddhist-art Lanna motifs carry through here. If you're arriving in Chiang Rai for the first time, starting right here makes sense — the Night Bazaar, cafés, and restaurants are all within easy walking distance.

The highlight you can't miss is the nightly light show. Every evening at 19:00, 20:00, and 21:00, the tower cycles through color-shifts from gold to pink, green, blue, and purple, while Chiang Rai Ramluk music plays underneath — each show runs about 10 minutes. Multiple reviews agree that the 20:00 show is the most impressive because the sky is fully dark by then and the colors pop more vividly than in the first round. During the day you can also visit — the intricate golden plasterwork covering the tower is worth seeing in full daylight — but the real draw is after dark.

Completely free, public space, no entry fee. No cost beyond travel and whatever you order at nearby food stalls or cafes. The most popular photo spot is directly across the roundabout from the tower, where you can frame the full structure. One practical note: the roundabout has active traffic flowing around it at all times, so take care when crossing the road or choosing where to stand. Some angles pick up power lines and lamp posts — move around to find a cleaner frame.

Popular because it packages everything into one spot — free, central, beautiful by day and night, with a scheduled show to anchor an evening. Works well for photography lovers, couples on evening strolls, or families wanting to watch something together before dinner. If you're coming for the show, arrive 10–15 minutes early to claim a good standing spot.
mustOrder: 20:00 light show — full dark sky, colors at their most vivid
Photograph the gold clock tower designed by Chalermchai
Golden plasterwork details in daylight
Continue on to the nearby Night Bazaar
blocks.hours: Open 24 hrs · light show at 19:00, 20:00, 21:00 daily

blocks.name: Hat Nakhon Chiang Rai Public Park (Tung and Khom Park)
blocks.area: Mueang Chiang Rai District (Kok River bank, near Mae Fa Luang Bridge)
blocks.signature: Wide riverfront park for walking and exercise, and the venue for the Chiang Rai Flower Festival in the cool season
blocks.descHtml:
Hat Nakhon Chiang Rai Public Park — which locals call simply Hat Chiang Rai — is a 100-rai-plus green space along the Kok River that the Chiang Rai city municipality transformed from neglected land into the city's breathing room. Located near Mae Fa Luang Bridge in Rob Wiang subdistrict, it's the place to go for anyone wanting to walk, run, or have a family picnic by the water without spending a single baht. The grounds stretch wide enough to walk for a full kilometer, with running tracks along the river, shaded trees, and open lawns where children can run freely.

The highlight that made this park famous is the late-year season, when it becomes the venue for the Chiang Rai Flower Festival — running continuously through more than 22 editions. The municipality plants over a million winter blooms including tulips, lilies, petunias, and many other varieties, with lights after dark and weekend live music. Multiple reviews describe the atmosphere as lush and spacious, with a large car park at the entrance. During the festival there are two performance stages, a food-and-souvenir zone, and easy strolling throughout.

Free entry all year round. Open daily approximately 07:00–21:00. Early mornings are fresh and good for a run; cool-season evenings during the Flower Festival are peak atmosphere — lights are on, the temperature is perfect, and the mood is upbeat. Easy to reach by car, with a wide parking area.

One thing to know: outside the flower festival season, the park runs as a normal public green space focused on walking, running, and relaxing rather than flower-viewing. If you're specifically coming for the blooms, check the Chiang Rai Flower Festival dates — typically December through February. Also note that the riverfront location means water levels can rise during heavy rain periods in the wet season — check conditions before visiting.
mustOrder: Chiang Rai Flower Festival in the cool season (tulips, lilies, lights)
Running and walking track along the Kok River
Weekend live music in the park
Riverside picnic under the trees
blocks.bestFor: Walking and running by the river, flower festival visit in the cool season

blocks.title: Book Chiang Rai tickets and tours — skip the queue
blocks.text: Chiang Rai's top attractions are spread across different parts of the city. If you're not driving yourself, booking a guided day tour through Klook or GetYourGuide that covers Wat Rong Khun, Wat Rong Suea Ten, Baan Dam Museum, and Singha Park in a single day is far more convenient than piecing it together yourself. Many packages include transport and entry tickets bundled together — book online in advance and skip the queue at the gate.

blocks.title: What to know before visiting Chiang Rai

items.title: Rent a car or use Grab
items.text: The main attractions are spread outside the center in different directions — renting a car or hiring a driver for the day is the most cost-effective option. Grab is available within the city, but coverage is limited at spots outside town. Pre-arrange a driver or join a tour for outlying sites.

items.title: Bring cash to the markets
items.text: The Walking Street and Night Bazaar food stalls mostly take cash. Carry small-denomination Thai baht notes. Entry fees for temples and museums are also most conveniently paid in cash.

items.title: Get to Wat Rong Khun early
items.text: Wat Rong Khun opens at 08:00 and tour buses from Chiang Mai typically arrive from mid-morning onward. Going right at opening means clean photos of the white ubosot without the crowd.

items.title: Dress modestly for temples
items.text: Wat Rong Khun and other temples require shoulders and knees covered, and shoes off before entering the ubosot. At Rong Khun, cover-up wraps are sometimes available to borrow — but in peak season they run out, so bringing your own sarong or overshirt is more reliable.

items.title: English is workable
items.text: Major attractions and tours have signs and staff who can communicate in English. At local markets and small roadside stalls, Thai is the main language — a translation app helps a lot.

items.title: Time your trip around Saturday
items.text: The Walking Street (Kad Jia Hay Ramluk) runs Saturday evenings only. If you can schedule your trip to include a Saturday night, you get the full northern Thai street food and folk-dance experience. Any other night, the Night Bazaar runs daily.

blocks.title: Plan your Chiang Rai trip to hit everything
blocks.html:
The most satisfying itinerary starts early at Wat Rong Khun — it opens at 08:00 and tour buses from Chiang Mai tend to arrive mid-morning through noon, so going right at opening means the white ubosot almost to yourself. From there, continue to Wat Rong Suea Ten and Baan Dam Museum, which sit on opposite sides of the city and can both be covered in half a day. Note that Baan Dam closes for lunch — time your arrival to avoid wasting the gap.

The afternoon is perfect for Singha Park's wide, breezy tea fields — ride the farm tour tram, taste the Oolong, and stretch your legs in the open air. As evening approaches, head back into the city. Wat Huay Pla Kang's lift closes around 18:00, so arriving before then gives you the city-view from the Guan Yin statue while the light is still soft. At night, if it's Saturday, the Walking Street on Thanalai Road is the move — a full kilometer of northern food and folk dancing. Any other night, the Night Bazaar is open and the Clock Tower light show runs at 19:00, 20:00, and 21:00.

blocks.text: Want to be at Wat Rong Khun before the crowds, or walk the Saturday Walking Street without a long drive back? Staying in central Chiang Rai makes the whole city loop much easier — hotels by the Kok River and near the Clock Tower cover a wide range of budgets.

faq.q: Which attractions in Chiang Rai should you not miss?
faq.a: For a first visit, the three spots people mention most are Wat Rong Khun (White Temple) — Chalermchai's all-white mirror-glass masterpiece — Wat Rong Suea Ten (Blue Temple) — cobalt blue and gold — and Singha Park with its broad tea fields. If you love art, add Baan Dam Museum by Thawan Duchanee.

faq.q: What are the highlights of Chiang Rai?
faq.a: Chiang Rai stands out for temples with genuinely unique design — Rong Khun in white and Rong Suea Ten in blue — plus the art of two National Artists: Chalermchai Kositpipat (Wat Rong Khun, Clock Tower) and Thawan Duchanee (Baan Dam). Other highlights are the cool climate, tea fields, evening markets, and the Walking Street.

faq.q: Are entry fees expensive for Chiang Rai attractions?
faq.a: Many sites are free — Wat Rong Suea Ten, the Clock Tower, and the Walking Street charge nothing. Wat Rong Khun is free for Thais; foreigners pay around 100 THB. Baan Dam Museum costs about 80 THB. Wat Huay Pla Kang is free but the lift inside the Guan Yin statue charges a small fee. Singha Park has free entry; trams and activities are priced separately.

faq.q: How do you get around Chiang Rai and is parking easy?
faq.a: The main attractions around Chiang Rai are all reachable by car. Wat Rong Khun, Singha Park, Baan Dam Museum, and Wat Huay Pla Kang all have large car parks. Renting a car or hiring a driver for the day is the most convenient option since the sites are spread in different directions. Within the old city — Clock Tower, Walking Street — you can walk between them, and Grab is available in town.

faq.q: What time do the attractions in Chiang Rai open?
faq.a: Wat Rong Khun opens from around 08:00 to 17:30. Baan Dam Museum opens 09:00 to 17:00 with a lunch break. Singha Park is open through the day until around 17:00 with the tram running until 17:00. Wat Huay Pla Kang opens early and stays open until evening, with the lift closing around 18:00. The Clock Tower has nightly light shows at 19:00, 20:00, and 21:00. The Walking Street is Saturday evenings only; the Night Bazaar opens every evening.
